partner_context.their_ambition: NYC Ferry, run for the city's Economic Development Corporation, operates the busiest urban ferry network in the US across the East River, Hudson and harbor — and the city is actively expanding water transit.
partner_context.their_pressure: The diesel catamaran fleet is speed- and range-limited (the Rockaway run is ~1 hr), wake complaints constrain East River operations, and fuel and emissions sit awkwardly with the city's climate goals — while road and subway capacity is maxed.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: A foiling fleet that runs faster, reaches the long outer-borough and regional routes the diesel cats can't economically serve, throws almost no wake on the East River, and decarbonizes the network.

hero.title: New York's waterways, foiling.
hero.subtitle: A faster, longer-range, lower-wake foiling layer for the nation's busiest urban ferry network.
hero.what_we_do_together: NYC's ferry operator and the EDC bring the routes, ridership and a city ringed by underused water; Navier brings a foiling fleet that runs faster, reaches farther, and throws almost no wake — opening new long-range routes the current diesel cats can't serve.

why_now: NYC is expanding ferry service, the city has aggressive climate mandates (Local Law 97), East River wake is a live constraint, and ~32M+ annual ferry trips prove the demand — the moment for a foiling layer is now.
multimodal_fit: New Yorkers already chain subway, bus, bike and ferry; a foiling pier slots into the same trip — subway to the waterfront, foil across the harbor, transit onward — adding fast water capacity where the subway can't reach.

proof_points.claim: NYC Ferry is the busiest US urban ferry network.
proof_points.evidence: ~32M+ annual trips across the East River, Hudson and harbor, with the city actively expanding service.

proof_points.claim: New York has aggressive climate mandates.
proof_points.evidence: Local Law 97 and citywide decarbonization goals create direct alignment for a zero-emission foiling fleet.

proof_points.claim: East River wake is a live operational constraint.
proof_points.evidence: Wake complaints limit speeds and routes; near-zero-wake foiling resolves the issue directly.

proof_points.claim: Subway and road capacity is maxed.
proof_points.evidence: With the subway and bridges at capacity, the surrounding water is New York's most underused right-of-way.

objections.concern: NYC Ferry is heavily subsidized already.
objections.response: Foiling improves the economics — faster turns, more trips per vessel, lower fuel — and opens revenue routes (long-range, regional) the diesel cats can't serve.

objections.concern: The harbor has heavy commercial traffic and ice risk.
objections.response: Software-defined routing manages traffic separation; foils ride above chop, and operations flex seasonally as the existing fleet already does.
We start with a demonstration on a flagship route (Rockaway long-haul or an East River wake-sensitive corridor) to prove the model before any fleet decision.

objections.concern: Accessibility and capacity standards are strict.
objections.response: The platform meets ADA and Coast Guard passenger standards; capacity is matched to route demand, supplementing rather than replacing high-capacity cats.

close.title: New York, on foils.
close.body: A faster, longer-range, near-wakeless foiling layer for NYC Ferry — halving the Rockaway run, ending East River wake complaints, and opening new regional routes.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling lifts the hull clear of the water, so a Navier vessel flies instead of plowing through chop - roughly 10x more efficient than a conventional planing boat, faster (30+ kt cruise), and dramatically smoother and quieter. It's software-defined and autonomy-ready, so the same fleet keeps getting better and cheaper to run over time. A step-change in marine mobility, not an incremental faster boat.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: Navier rides on infrastructure that already exists - the open ocean and the berths and jetties already in use. No vertiports, no new rights-of-way, no tunnels or tracks. Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal; the Quanta-LR hybrid needs no charging infrastructure at all. That's the fundamental contrast with flying taxis and other new-infrastructure modes: nothing to permit, build, or wait for.
why_navier_now.the_moment: NYC's ferry expansion, Local Law 97 climate mandates, chronic congestion, and live East River wake constraints converge — a faster, zero-wake, zero-emission foiling fleet answers all four at once.

ladder_transitions.basis: Two-lever step. (1) Faster, more comfortable boats grow the cross-water market (induced demand). (2) Leading-operator capture lifts share from 10% floor to 25% mature, network-wide.
